solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Son tucked into much loved duck and Italian sauce

indicators.note: the son is tucked inside the pet, as a child into bed

parts.note: a pet is a much-loved favourite
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A menu: duck served with an Italian sauce, and a son happily tucking in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' looks like the meat course, but it is the cricketer's zero. S goes inside PET, and O is added at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Pesto is the basil-and-pine-nut sauce from Genoa.

clue.text: Country's body of water containing algae regularly avoided

indicators.note: the pond holds the other letters inside it

parts.note: a pond is a small body of water

indicators.note: every other letter of 'algae' is skipped, keeping L and A

parts.note: skip A, G and E in a-L-g-A-e, leaving L and A

explanation.surface: A nation's lake kept clear of pond scum.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'has', linking the country to the wordplay. LA sits between PO and ND.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Poland is one country among many in central Europe.

clue.text: Disease's evidence of harm felt wrong always

indicators.note: the letters of 'felt' are put the wrong way round

parts.note: a scar is the mark an injury leaves

explanation.surface: A patient describing a disease: visible damage, and it always felt wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'has' and links the definition to the wordplay. 'Felt' looks like a verb about feeling ill, but it only supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Scarlet fever is a bacterial infection with a red rash, mostly in children.

clue.text: In public view, Dicky rides unfancied racehorse

indicators.note: dicky means shaky or unsound, so the letters of 'rides' are out of order

parts.note: something that is out is openly known

explanation.surface: A jockey named Dicky riding a long shot where everyone can see.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dicky' looks like a jockey's name; it is the British adjective for shaky or unsound, used here to mix up RIDES.
explanation.definitionFit: An outsider is a horse given little chance of winning.

clue.text: Peculiar drink raised commotion

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting a word turns it bottom to top

parts.note: rum = odd, in old-fashioned British speech

explanation.surface: A strange drink stirred up a fuss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peculiar drink' reads as one phrase, suggesting rum as the drink itself; in fact 'Peculiar' gives RUM and 'drink' gives SUP.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words mean a noisy fuss or uproar.

clue.text: Initially, Ben uncovers Rolls Royce's humming sound

indicators.note: take the first letters of the next two words

parts.note: first letters of Ben and uncovers
RR is the badge of Rolls-Royce

explanation.surface: Ben pulls off a car cover to reveal a purring Rolls-Royce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uncovers' looks like the verb of the scene, but it only lends its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A burr is a low whirring or humming noise.

clue.text: Picked up this writer covering part of Observer?

indicators.note: heard, as a radio picks up a signal

explanation.surface: A journalist spotted writing for part of the Observer newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Observer is a British Sunday newspaper, but here it is just anyone who observes, whose eyelid is part of them; the question mark flags the trick.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyelid is part of the eye of whoever is looking.

clue.text: French one meets American university supporter rarely

explanation.surface: A Frenchman seldom meets a fan of an American college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'American university' looks like one phrase, perhaps a college name, but splits into US and U.
explanation.definitionFit: Unusually and rarely both mean not often, in 'not unusually cold'.

clue.text: Canadian singer-songwriter played chord alone, half seen

indicators.note: the letters are played around with, like notes
only one half of 'seen' is used

explanation.surface: A singer-songwriter strums a single chord on stage, half in view.
explanation.walkthrough: The musical surface fits the answer neatly: 'played' and 'chord' are just what Leonard Cohen did, which disguises the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonard Cohen was the Canadian writer of 'Hallelujah' and 'Suzanne'.

clue.text: Jumped as plate smashed

indicators.note: the plate breaks and its letters are pieced together differently

explanation.surface: Someone jumped at the sound of a plate smashing.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a plain scene of alarm, so 'smashed' reads as what happened to the plate rather than an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Leapt is a past tense of leap, to jump.

clue.text: Fantastic winger's big match in US

parts.note: a winger here is a bird

explanation.surface: A brilliant footballer on the wing plays in a big American game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winger' is a wide player in football, but here anything with wings; the obvious break after SUPER is the wrong one.
explanation.definitionFit: The Super Bowl is the championship game of American football.

clue.text: Outstanding musical performance of couple shortened

indicators.note: the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a duet is a piece for two performers

explanation.surface: Praise for a superb duet that was cut short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding' looks like praise for the performance, but it means unpaid, as a bill is outstanding.
explanation.definitionFit: The money sense: a bill still unpaid is both outstanding and owed.

clue.text: Panel of vehicle mum found in terribly bad road

indicators.note: the letters of 'bad road' are badly jumbled
the silencing word sits inside the others

parts.note: mum = silent, as in 'keep mum'; SH asks for quiet

explanation.surface: A car's instrument panel goes quiet on a rough road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mum' looks like mother, the usual MA, but here it means silent, as in 'keep mum'.
explanation.definitionFit: The dashboard is the panel of instruments in front of a driver.

clue.text: Giant winged insect under hebe fluttered

indicators.note: the letters of 'hebe' flap about into a new order
in a down clue, the moth goes below the other part

parts.note: a moth is a winged insect

explanation.surface: A huge moth flutters beneath a hebe bush in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: A hebe is a common garden shrub, which makes 'fluttered' look like the moth's movement rather than an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A behemoth is something enormous, from the biblical beast.

clue.text: Do a makeover on hair and blunder

parts.note: bish is British slang for a mistake

explanation.surface: A hairdresser gives a makeover and makes a mess of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On hair' reads as the makeover's target, but 'on' is RE. Bish is an informal British word for a blunder.
explanation.definitionFit: Renovating a room or building gives it a makeover, the property sense of the word.

clue.text: Florid Australian native going round business clubs

indicators.note: the kangaroo's letters surround the others

explanation.surface: A flamboyant Australian doing the rounds of business clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Australian native' suggests an Aborigine, but it is the kangaroo; CO and C sit inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Rococo is the highly ornate 18th-century style, so florid.

clue.text: Single working Scotsman related to Ancient Greeks

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
a machine that is on is working
Ian is the Scottish form of John

explanation.surface: An unmarried Scot in work who is descended from the Greeks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Single' reads as unmarried, but it is the numeral I.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ionians were one of the main tribes of ancient Greece.

clue.text: Hideout finally had more protection

indicators.note: take the final letter of each of the next words

parts.note: last letters of haD, morE, protectioN

explanation.surface: A hideout that at last offered better shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' reads as 'at last' in the story, which hides that it applies to each of the three words after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A den is a secret hiding place.

clue.text: Knight in charge, see, in a pleasant way

parts.note: a see is a bishop's diocese; Ely is a cathedral city in England

explanation.surface: A knight in command courteously invites someone to look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like the verb, but it is a bishop's diocese; Ely is the one crosswords use most.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb of nice, so the definition is an adverbial phrase of the same meaning.

clue.text: Beware of dog with stick originally muzzled behind hole in rock

indicators.note: take the first letter of 'muzzled'

parts.note: a cave is a hollow in rock
a cane is a walking stick

explanation.surface: A dog warning: the animal is muzzled and kept in a cave with a stick.
explanation.walkthrough: The dog-themed surface (muzzled, stick) fits the answer, the Latin warning found in a Pompeii mosaic.
explanation.definitionFit: Cave canem is Latin for 'beware of the dog'.

clue.text: Imbecile Conservative group

parts.note: a lot is a group or batch

explanation.surface: A jibe calling a Tory faction idiots.
explanation.walkthrough: Clot is a mild British insult for a foolish person.
explanation.definitionFit: A mild British insult for a stupid person, so a synonym in everyday slang.

clue.text: Brownish-yellow brooch restored somewhat

indicators.note: only some of the words' letters are used

explanation.surface: A tarnished brooch, partly restored to a yellowish-brown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Restored' looks like a signal to rearrange, but the letters run in order across the word break.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of an earth pigment, and hence of its colour.

clue.text: Motor car crashed trapping northern seabird

indicators.note: the motor car's letters are wrecked into a new order

explanation.surface: A car crash on a northern road pins a seabird.
explanation.walkthrough: N goes in before the final T.
explanation.definitionFit: A cormorant is a large dark diving seabird.

clue.text: Harry's outside hugging somebody dear

indicators.note: only the outer letters of Harry are kept
the outer letters wrap round the other word

parts.note: first and last letters of Harry
one = someone, as in 'one never knows'

explanation.surface: Harry is outdoors embracing a loved one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harry's outside' reads as 'Harry is outdoors', but it means Harry's outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Honey and dear are both terms of endearment.
